transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because… I don’t know, it’s hard to explain without sounding ridiculous. I teach secondary school, and we’ve been using these lesson videos, and when I see myself on them, all I can focus on is this one side of my face. It looks crooked to me, sort of swollen-looking, like it’s all anyone would notice.

And then I’m in class thinking the students are staring at it, or parents if they see a video, or staff in meetings… not listening to what I’m saying, just looking at my face. I know I’m supposed to be talking about work or lessons, but once I notice it, I can’t get past it.
Does this concern about your appearance cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your work, relationships, or other areas of your life?

Yes. It’s… it’s become a real problem at work. I’ll sit down to do lesson planning and then somehow I’ve lost ages thinking about how I’ll look in front of the class, or whether a video angle makes it worse, and the actual planning just doesn’t get done.

I’m behind on lesson plans, mentoring stuff, even the basketball coaching I help with. And I used to be pretty on top of things, you know? I mean, I’d stay late marking or setting up drills, and now I’m missing deadlines. Administrators have started writing things down—missed deadlines, problems with coverage—and I’m honestly scared I’m close to losing my position.
Can you describe what you see on your face that concerns you? Have others noticed it or commented on it?

It’s mainly this one side of my face. On the videos it looks… crooked, like it’s sort of swollen compared with the other side. I’ll be trying to watch the lesson back for teaching reasons, you know, whether the explanation made sense, but then I’m not listening to myself at all—I’m just staring at that side of my face.

I don’t know if people have actually said anything directly. That’s the thing, no one comes up and says, “Your face looks strange,” but I feel like they must notice. The students, parents if they see the videos, staff in meetings… I feel like they’re looking at it instead of hearing what I’m saying.
Have you ever asked someone else, like a friend or family member, if they notice this crookedness or swelling on your face, and what did they say?

I mean… I’ve tried to bring it up, sort of, but I don’t think I ask it very clearly because then I feel embarrassed. It’s this one side of my face, especially on the lesson videos—it looks crooked and kind of swollen to me, and once I see it, I can’t stop seeing it.

And then I’m thinking, well, if I can see it that clearly, surely the students can, and parents if they watch the videos, and other staff in meetings. They must be staring at that instead of listening to what I’m saying. I know that’s not exactly answering what they said back, but it’s hard because even if someone says it’s fine, I still see it.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking your face in mirrors, avoiding certain angles, or seeking reassurance about your appearance?

Yes, I do. Especially with anything on camera. Before I post a recorded lesson, or if I’ve got a parent conference online, I’ll keep moving the laptop around, changing the angle, checking how that side of my face looks.

Then I replay little clips over and over, and sometimes I’ll sort of cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks less obvious. It’s ridiculous because I’m supposed to be checking the lesson content, but I end up re-recording the whole thing again and again.

And then suddenly I’m late for class or I haven’t done the prep I needed to do. I used to be really organised with that stuff, like I’d have resources ready and everything, but now the camera thing just eats up all the time.
Is your concern specifically about the appearance of your face, particularly its asymmetry and swelling, or are you also worried about other parts of your body or physical features?

It’s mostly my face, yes. That one side that looks crooked or sort of swollen on the lesson videos. I mean, I notice other things now and then like anyone does, but that’s not why I’m here.

The thing I can’t get past is seeing my face on camera and then thinking the students must be noticing it, or parents if they watch, or staff in meetings. Like they’re staring at that instead of listening to what I’m actually saying. And then I lose track of everything else, even the lesson.
Have you ever wondered if there might be a reason others aren’t commenting on your face, like maybe they’re trying not to hurt your feelings or are avoiding the topic on purpose?

Yeah, I do think that sometimes… like maybe they’re just being polite or they don’t want to make it awkward. But then I sort of go round in circles with it, because I’m here because I can’t stop seeing it myself — that crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos.

And once I’ve noticed it, I start thinking the students must be seeing it too, and the parents if they watch the videos, and staff in meetings… like they’re all staring at that instead of listening to what I’m actually saying. Then even if no one comments, that almost makes me wonder more, if that makes sense.

When you're focused on how your face looks on camera, is it more like you're trying to fix or hide a flaw you believe is unacceptable, or is it more about not being able to be sure that others won't notice it and judge you for it?

I think it’s… I mean, it’s both in a way, but mainly I just can’t stop seeing it once it’s on the screen. That crooked, swollen-looking side of my face, especially in the lesson videos.

And then my mind goes off with it — like the students must be noticing it, or the parents watching later, or staff in meetings. I start thinking they’re staring at that instead of listening to what I’m actually saying. Then I’m not even thinking about the lesson anymore, I’m just stuck on my face.
How much time would you say you spend each day thinking about how your face looks on camera or worrying that others are noticing it?

It’s… a lot of the day, honestly. I don’t always sit there with a stopwatch or anything, but once I’ve seen myself on one of the lesson videos, it keeps coming back.

Like I’ll be marking or planning, or even just making a cup of tea in the staff room, and suddenly I’m thinking about that crooked, swollen-looking side of my face again. Then I start imagining the students noticing it, or parents watching the recording, or people in staff meetings looking at that instead of listening to what I’m saying.

So I don’t know the exact number, but it feels like it takes up hours, not just a few minutes.
Has this preoccupation with your face ever led to moments where you felt so anxious or upset that you had trouble functioning normally, even outside of work?

Yeah… it’s not just at work exactly, though work is where it shows up most clearly. I’ll get so wound up about the videos or how I looked in a meeting that I just sort of lose hours, and then nothing gets finished.

I’ve fallen behind on lesson planning, mentoring stuff, and even basketball coaching things I’m meant to organise. And I used to be pretty on top of all that — I mean, I’ve always been the person who had the drills ready, the seating plans, all of it. Now deadlines slip because I’m stuck replaying how my face looked or trying to avoid seeing myself again.

The administrators have started writing things down, missed deadlines and coverage problems. That’s the part that scares me. It feels like I’m getting close to losing my position, and then I think, well, that would be ridiculous, losing my job because I can’t stop thinking about my face on a screen… but it doesn’t stop it happening.
